Announcements - Statistical Inference/Hypothesis Testing Continued - Discussion of Final Projects and Friday's Lab ## Announcements - Lab 11 this week - give and receive feedback on your projects. - Final 2 lectures (Wednesday, Monday) - course review. - [Assignment 4](https://josephessig-source.github.io/pols1600_site/assignments/a4.html) due Sunday April 19th - Next Wednesday, April 22, Work on converting draft into presentation # {{< fa magnifying-glass>}} Review {.inverse} ## Sampling Distributions and Standard Errors {.smaller} - A sampling distribution is a theoretical probability distribution of estimates obtained from taking repeated samples of size $n$ from some population - A distribution of what we could have seen - A standard error is simply the standard deviation ($\sigma$) of the sampling distribution of an estimator. - A measure of how much our estimate could have varied. - Law of Large Numbers: As $N \to \infty$ $\bar{x} \to \mu$ - Central Limit Theorem: As $N \to \infty$ $\bar{x} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \frac{\sigma^2}{n})$ ## Confidence Intervals {.smaller} > Confidence intervals provide a range of plausible values for our estimate - Three components: - Point Estimate (i.e. a mean, or coefficient) - Confidence Level (Often 95 percent by convention) - Margin of Error (+/- some range (typically 1.96\*SE for 95 percent CI)) - Confidence is about the interval - 95 percent of the intervals constructed in this manner would contain the true parameter in repeated samples. ## Hypothesis Testing {.smaller} - A hypothesis test quantifies how likely it is that we would observe what we did (our test statistic), if some claim about the world were true (our hypothesis, typically a null ). - If our claim were true, then [under this null hypothesis]{.blue}, our test statistic would have a distribution centered around the null value. - A [p-value]() which describes the probability of observing a test statistic as extreme or more extreme in a world where our null hypothesis was true - If our [p-value is small]{.blue} ($p < 0.05$), we [reject the null]{.blue} hypothesis If our [p-value is large]{.blue} ($p > 0.05$), we [fail to reject the null]{.blue}, or retain the null hypothesis ## {.smaller} #### Relationship between CIs and Hypothesis Testing :::: panel-tabset ## Concept We can think of a confidence interval as a [range of hypotheses we would fail to reject]{.blue} with $p < \alpha$ If a $95\%$ confidence interval excludes 0, the corresponding two-sided hypothesis test will reject at $\alpha = 0.05$ ## {{}} Code ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Load Data load(url("https://josephessig-source.github.io/pols1600_site/files/data/nes24.rda")) # Fit Model m1 <- lm_robust(dv_participation ~ education + income, df, se = "classical") # Range of hypotheses for education pval_ci_df <- tibble( # Hypothesized Betas for Education Hypothesis = seq(0, .32, length.out = 100), # Test Statistics Statistic = (m1$coefficients["education"] - Hypothesis) / m1$std.error["education"], # P-value for two sided test `p-value` = 2*pt(abs(Statistic), df = m1$df,lower.tail = F) ) fig_pval_ci <- pval_ci_df %>% ggplot(aes(Hypothesis, `p-value`))+ geom_line()+ geom_vline(xintercept = m1$coefficients["education"], linetype = "solid", col = "red")+ geom_vline(xintercept = m1$conf.low["education"], linetype = "dotted")+ geom_vline(xintercept = m1$conf.high["education"], linetype = "dotted")+ geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed")+ labs( x = "Hypothesized Education, Coefficent", title = "Confidence intervals are a range\nof plausible hypotheses" )+ theme_minimal() ``` ::: ## {{}} Table

## {{}} Figure ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](11-slides_files/figure-revealjs/fig_pval_ci-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: :::: ## Four Possible Outcomes of a hypothesis Test {.smaller} ::::{.columns} :::{.column width=45%} - **False Positive: (Type I Error)** - Rejecting a True $H_0$. - $\tau = 0$, but $\hat{\tau}$ has a $p<0.05$ - Probability=$\alpha$ - **True Positive: (Correct Decision)** - Rejecting a false $H_0$: - $\tau \neq 0$, and $\hat{\tau}$ has a $p<0.05$ - Occurs with Probability = $1-\beta$ ::: :::{.column width=45%} - **True Negative: (Correct Decision) ** - Failing to reject a True $H_0$: - $\tau = 0$, and $\hat{\tau}$ has a $p>0.05$ - Occurs with Probability = $1-\alpha$ - **False Negative: (Type II Error)** - Failing to reject a false $H_0$. - $\tau \neq 0$ but $\hat{\tau}$ has a $p>0.05$ - Occurs with Probability= $\beta$ ::: :::: ## Type 1 and 2 Errors ![](https://miro.medium.com/max/1400/1*uF5aBZ63BZ8IDEyF8wo-CA.png) [Source](https://towardsdatascience.com/a-general-guidance-of-hypothesis-testing-7cab119ca999) # Statistical Power ## Statistical Power ```{webr-r} #| label: plot_power #| context: setup power_function <- function(tau = 2, se =1, pval = 0.05){ df <- tibble( x = seq(-4*se, tau+4*se,length.out = 100 ), p = dnorm(x, mean = 0, sd = se) ) the_x_min <- min(c(min(df$x), -5)) the_x_max <- max(max(df$x), 7) the_y_max <- max(df$p) z <- qnorm(1-(pval/2), sd = se) power <- pnorm(z, mean = tau, sd =se, lower.tail = F) type2_error <- pnorm(z, mean = tau, sd =se) if(power > type2_error){ the_y_power <- dnorm(z, mean = tau, sd = se)*.7 the_y_type2 <- dnorm(z, mean = tau, sd = se)*.3 } if(power <= type2_error){ the_y_power <- dnorm(z, mean = tau, sd = se)*.3 the_y_type2 <- dnorm(z, mean = tau, sd = se)*.7 } fig_power <- df %>% ggplot(aes(x))+ ylim(0,the_y_max + the_y_max/10)+ xlim(the_x_min, the_x_max)+ stat_function(geom = "line", fun = dnorm, args = list(sd = se), alpha = 0.5)+ stat_function(geom = "line", fun = dnorm, alpha = 0.5, col = "blue", args =list(mean = tau, sd = se))+ stat_function(geom = "area", fun = dnorm, fill = "darkblue", alpha = 0.5, xlim = c(the_x_min,qnorm(1-(pval/2),sd = se)), args =list(mean = tau, sd = se))+ stat_function(geom = "area", fun = dnorm, fill = "lightblue", alpha = 0.7, xlim = c(qnorm(1-(pval/2), sd = se),the_x_max), args =list(mean = tau, sd = se))+ stat_function(geom = "area", fun = dnorm, fill = "red", alpha = .25, xlim = c(qnorm(1-(pval/2), sd = se),the_x_max), args =list(mean = 0, sd = se) )+ stat_function(geom = "area", fun = dnorm, fill = "red", alpha = .5, xlim = c(qnorm(pval/2,sd = se),the_x_min), args =list(mean = 0, sd = se) )+ geom_vline(xintercept = qnorm(1-(pval/2),sd = se), linetype =2)+ geom_segment( data = tibble(x = 0, xend= tau, y = the_y_max, yend = the_y_max), aes(x = x, xend = xend, y=y, yend=yend) )+ annotate("text", x = tau/2, y = the_y_max + the_y_max/40, label = expression(tau), hjust=.5)+ annotate("text", x = -z-se/10, y = the_y_max*.02, label = expression( paste(alpha,"/2", sep ="")), hjust=1 )+ annotate("text", x = z+se/10, y = the_y_max*.02, label = expression( paste(alpha,"/2", sep ="")), hjust=0 )+ annotate("text", x = z-se/8, y = the_y_type2-the_y_max/20, label = expression(beta), hjust=1) + annotate("text", x = z-se/8, y = the_y_type2, label = "Type II-Error", hjust=1)+ annotate("text", x = z+se/8, y = the_y_power, label = paste( "Statistical Power = ", round(power,2),sep = ""), hjust=0)+ annotate("text", x = z+se/8, y = the_y_power-the_y_max/20, label = expression(paste("1-",beta,sep="")), hjust=0)+ annotate("text", x = 0, y = the_y_max + the_y_max/40, label = expression(H[0]), hjust=0.5)+ annotate("text", x = tau, y = the_y_max + the_y_max/40, label = expression(H[1]), hjust=0.5)+ annotate("text", x = z+se/8, y = the_y_max + the_y_max/10, label = "z=critical value", hjust=0)+ theme_void() return(fig_power) } ``` :::: panel-tabset ## Concept :::{.nonincremental} - Consider two distributions of statistics under - a null of no effect ($H_0$) - an effect of $\tau$ ($H_1$) - For a significance threshold of $\alpha$ we would: - Fail to reject the null $\beta$ (Type II Errors) - Correctly reject the null $1 -\beta$ (Statistical Power) ::: ## Power Try changing $\tau$ (the effect size), and se (the standard deviation of the effect) ```{webr-r} #| label: power #| autorun: true #| context: interactive #| message: false power_function(tau = 2, se = 1, pval = 0.05) ``` ## Comments Power is a function of: - Sample size ($N$) - Larger samples, smaller standard errors (LLN) - Effect size ($\tau$) - Bigger effects less overlap - Significance threshold ($\alpha$) - Decrease Type 1 (False Positives) error leads to increased Type 2 (False Negatives) - The distribution of the data - Variance, asymptotic approximations :::: ## Paths to Statistical Inference {.smaller} Whether we use math, bootstrapping, or shuffling, the goal of statistical inference is exactly the same: quantifying our uncertainty. - **1. Asymptotic Inference** - We use the Central Limit Theorem and to *assume* a theoretical distribution (like the $t$-distribution). - Compare the observed test statistic to the assumed sampling distribution under the null. - **Best for:** Large samples with well-behaved data. Very fast. - **2. Bootstrapping (Using Resampling)** - We draw new samples *with replacement* from our data to mimic drawing new samples from the population. - Compare the observed test statistic to the *empirical* approximation of the sampling distribution. - **Best for:** Constructing **Confidence Intervals** and Standard Errors without relying on strict assumptions. - **3. Randomization Inference (Permutation)** - We shuffle the treatment labels *without replacement* to simulate a world where the treatment has no effect. - Centers on the *null hypothesis*. - **Best for:** Calculating exact **$p$-values** and testing hypotheses, especially in experiments with small samples. # {{< fa mug-hot >}} Randomization Inference {.inverse} ## The Lady Tasting Tea {.smaller} - **The Claim:** In the 1920s, Dr. Muriel Bristol claimed she could taste whether milk or tea was poured into her cup first. - **The Experiment:** Ronald Fisher prepared 8 cups of tea. - 4 had milk poured first. - 4 had tea poured first. - The cups were presented in a random, blinded order. - **The Task:** Identify the 4 cups that had milk poured first. - **The Null Hypothesis (**$H_0$**):** She has no tasting ability; she is just guessing blindly. ## Permutations {.smaller} - If she is just guessing ($H_0$ is true), her choices are completely independent of the actual cups. - How many possible ways can she choose 4 cups out of 8? $$ \binom{8}{4} = \frac{8!}{4!(8-4)!} = 70 $$ - If she is guessing blindly, every one of these 70 combinations is equally likely. - If she gets all 4 correct, what is the probability of that happening by chance? **1/70 ≈ 0.014**. - Because **0.014 < 0.05**, we [reject the null hypothesis]{.blue}! ## {.smaller} #### ## Simulating the Null Distribution We can simulate this process in R by randomly shuffling (permuting) the "Milk First" labels while holding her guesses constant, we generate a [distribution of the test statistic under the null]{.blue}. This is exactly what we do in randomization inference. ## {{< fa code >}} Code ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # 1. Setup the actual truth (4 milk, 4 tea) truth <- c(rep("Milk", 4), rep("Tea", 4)) # 2. Assume she got them all right (her guesses exactly match the truth) lady_guesses <- c(rep("Milk", 4), rep("Tea", 4)) # 3. Create a function to simulate one random guess simulate_guess <- function() { shuffled_truth <- sample(truth, replace = FALSE) # Calculate test statistic: number of correctly identified "Milk" cups correct_milk <- sum(shuffled_truth == "Milk" & lady_guesses == "Milk") return(correct_milk) } # 4. Repeat 10,000 times to build the null distribution set.seed(1600) null_distribution <- tibble( sim = 1:10000, correct_milk = replicate(10000, simulate_guess()) ) # 5. Plot fig_tea <- null_distribution %>% ggplot(aes(x = correct_milk)) + geom_bar(fill = "grey60", color = "black") + geom_vline(xintercept = 4, color = "red", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) + theme_minimal() + scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:4) + labs( title = "Null Distribution of Correct 'Milk First' Guesses", subtitle = "Red dashed line indicates observed test statistic (4 correct)", x = "Number of Correct 'Milk First' Guesses", y = "Frequency" ) ``` ::: ## Plot ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](11-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-1-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Comments - The bar chart represents the sampling distribution of our test statistic if the null hypothesis were true (she is randomly guessing). - The red line represents our observed test statistic (she guessed all 4 correctly). - Notice how rare it is to get 4 correct by chance! Only about 1.4% of our 10,000 simulations resulted in 4 correct guesses. This simulation matches the exact math (1/70 = 0.014), yielding a $p$-value of 0.014. ## Putting It All Together {.smaller} - **Inference is about uncertainty:** We only have one sample, but we want to learn about the population. - **Standard Errors:** Tell us how much our estimate would vary if we took new samples. - **Confidence Intervals:** Give us a plausible range for the true population parameter based on our sample estimate and its standard error. - **Hypothesis Testing & P-values:** Help us quantify the evidence against a specific baseline claim (the null hypothesis $H_0$). - **Power:** Reminds us that sample size and effect size dictate our ability to detect the truth. # {{< fa lightbulb>}} Final Projects {.inverse} ## Structure of Final Paper and Drafts {.smaller} [Assignment 4:](https://josephessig-source.github.io/pols1600_site/assignments/a4.html) Seven sections 1. Introduction (5 percent, \~ 4 paragraphs) 2. Theory and Expectations (10 percent, \~4+ paragraphs) 3. Data (20 percent \~ 4+ paragraphs) 4. Design (25 percent \~ 5+ paragraphs) 5. Results (25 percent \~ 5+ paragraphs) 6. Conclusion (5 percent \~ 3+ paragraphs) 7. Appendix (10 percent \~ Variable codebook and all the R code for your project) ## For Friday {.smaller} - [Download template](https://josephessig-source.github.io/pols1600_site/assignments/pols1600_paper_template.qmd) - Make progress on: - 3. **Data** (20 percent \~ 4+ paragraphs) - 4. **Design** (25 percent \~ 5+ paragraphs) - 5. **Results** (25 percent \~ 5+ paragraphs) ## For Friday {.smaller} See [Lab 11 - Peer Workshop on Final Papers](https://josephessig-source.github.io/pols1600_site/labs/11-lab.qmd) You are not expected to have a full draft of your paper. Instead, your group should be prepared to briefly explain: - Your research question - Your main hypothesis (what you expect to find) - Your data source(s) - Your key variables (dependent + main independent variable(s)) - Your planned empirical strategy (what models or comparisons you will run) - **One area where you feel uncertain or would like feedback** The HTML files you submitted for assignments 2 and 3 should be helpful here, and you may want to present them (or parts of them) in addition to a verbal discussion. # {{< fa magnifying-glass>}} Course Review {.inverse} ## Types of inference - Descriptive - Causal - Predictive ## Descriptive Inference {.smaller} > Summarize distributions and relationships in data - You should know how to: - [Calculate](https://josephessig-source.github.io/pols1600_site/slides/01-slides#/using-r-to-summarize-data) and interpret measures: - Central Tendency - Dispersion - Association - [Load](https://josephessig-source.github.io/pols1600_site/slides/01-slides#/loading-data-into-r), [look at](https://josephessig-source.github.io/pols1600_site/slides/01-slides#/looking-at-your-data), [wrangle](https://josephessig-source.github.io/pols1600_site/slides/01-slides#/dplyr-functions-for-data-wrangling), and [describe](https://josephessig-source.github.io/pols1600_site/slides/01-slides#/describing-data-in-r) data using: - Tables - Figures ## Data Wrangling {.smaller} > The process of transforming data into a useable format You should know how to: - Load, look at,and transform data into R - Get a [HLO](https://josephessig-source.github.io/pols1600_site/slides/01-slides#/hlos-allow-you-to) of the raw data: - Unit of observation - Dimensions of the data - Quickly summarize the distributions and values of variables - [Recode](https://josephessig-source.github.io/pols1600_site/labs/07-lab-comments.html#recode-covariates) data to: - Replace values as `NA`s - Create categories, indicators (0,1), and factors - Transform predictors (e.g. standardizing predictors) - Reshape the data - Pivoting columns and rows - Joining data sets together. - [Aggregate](https://josephessig-source.github.io/pols1600_site/labs/02-lab-comments#reproduce-the-figure-from-lab-01) the data into [summaries](https://josephessig-source.github.io/pols1600_site/labs/03-lab-comments#calculate-the-average-treatment-effect) ## Data Visualization{.smaller} > A tool for describing distributions and relationships You should know: - The [grammar of graphics](https://josephessig-source.github.io/pols1600_site/slides/02-slides#/the-grammar-of-graphics): - Data - Aesthetic mappings - Geometries - How to [generate common plots](https://josephessig-source.github.io/pols1600_site/slides/02-slides#/describing-distributions-and-associations) to describe: - Distributions - Relationships ## Causal Inference{.smaller} > Causal Inference requires counterfactual comparisons You should know: - [Potential outcomes](https://josephessig-source.github.io/pols1600_site/slides/03-slides#/potential-outcomes-notation) and [DAGs](https://josephessig-source.github.io/pols1600_site/slides/04-slides.html#/directed-acyclic-graphs) - The [fundamental problem of causal inference](https://josephessig-source.github.io/pols1600_site/slides/03-slides#/fundamental-problem-of-causal-inference) - Bias caused by: - [Confounding](https://josephessig-source.github.io/pols1600_site/slides/04-slides.html#/section) (Coffee and Cancer) - [Colliding](https://josephessig-source.github.io/pols1600_site/slides/04-slides.html#/section-1) (Dating Jerks) - Casual Identification in: - [Experimental](https://josephessig-source.github.io/pols1600_site/slides/03-slides#/causal-identification-with-experimental-designs) designs - [Observational](https://josephessig-source.github.io/pols1600_site/slides/04-slides.html#/causal-inference-in-observational-studies) designs - [The Average Treatment Effect (ATE)](https://josephessig-source.github.io/pols1600_site/slides/03-slides#/estimating-an-average-treatment-effect) ## Prediction with Linear Models {.smaller} > Linear regression provides a linear estimate of the conditional expectation function You should know: - [How linear regression works](https://josephessig-source.github.io/pols1600_site/slides/05-slides#/understanding-linear-regression) - [What it means to control for](https://josephessig-source.github.io/pols1600_site/slides/07-slides.html#/regression-models-partition-variance) predictors in a multiple regression - How to translate [substantive claims]{.blue} into [empirical expectations](https://josephessig-source.github.io/pols1600_site/labs/06-lab-comments#estimate-a-model-controlling-for-age) for our models - How to [estimate and interpret]{.blue} these models using [tables](https://josephessig-source.github.io/pols1600_site/labs/06-lab-comments#display-the-model-as-a-regression-table) and [figures](https://josephessig-source.github.io/pols1600_site/slides/10-slides.html#/predicted-values) - How to [quantify uncertainty]{.blue} about these estimates using [confidence intervals](https://josephessig-source.github.io/pols1600_site/slides/10-slides#/confidence-intervals-1) and [hypothesis tests](https://josephessig-source.github.io/pols1600_site/slides/10-slides#/what-is-a-hypothesis-test). ## Probability {.smaller} - [Probability](https:/josephessig-source.github.io/pols1600_site/slides/08-slides#/probability-1) describes the likelihood of an event - [Random variables](https://josephessig-source.github.io/pols1600_site/slides/08-slides#/random-variables) assign numeric values to all the events that could occur. - [Probability distributions](https://josephessig-source.github.io/pols1600_site/slides/08-slides#/probability-distributions) assign probabilities to every value of a random variable. Can be: - discrete - continuous - characterized by their expected values and variances - used to: - describe the [data generating process]{.blue} - [quantify uncertainty]{.blue} about estimates ## Regression ## Controlling for Variables & Residualized Regression {.smaller} > Regression models partition the variance in the outcome into variance explained by the model and unexplained variance (residuals) You should know: - [The logic of residualized regression.](https://josephessig-source.github.io/pols1600_site/slides/07-slides.html#/residualized-regression) You can isolate the effect of $X_1$ on $Y$ by regressing the residuals of $Y$ (unexplained by $X_2$) on the residuals of $X_1$ (unexplained by $X_2$). - [Properties of Residuals:](https://josephessig-source.github.io/pols1600_site/slides/07-slides.html#/residuals-are-uncorrelated-with-x-and-haty) Residuals ($\hat{\epsilon}$) are orthogonal to (uncorrelated with) both the predictors and the predicted values. - [Why coefficients change](https://josephessig-source.github.io/pols1600_site/slides/07-slides.html#/why-did-the-coefficient-on-rep-vote-share-change-in-m3-but-not-m2) Controlling for a new variable only changes the coefficient of an existing predictor if the new variable is correlated with both the predictor and the outcome. ## Predictions and Model Fit {.smaller} > Regression coefficients define a formula to generate predicted values, while fit statistics summarize how well the model explains the data You should know: - **Generating predictions:** How to use `expand_grid()` to hold variables constant and `predict()` to generate expected values, which is especially useful for interpreting polynomials or interaction terms. - **R-squared ($R^2$):** The proportion of variance in the outcome explained by the model ($ESS/TSS$). - **Standardization:** Why we convert variables to z-scores (mean 0, standard deviation 1) to compare coefficients on a common scale. ## Difference-in-Differences (DiD) {.smaller} > Diff in Diff estimates causal effects by comparing the change in outcomes over time between a treated group and a control group You should know: - **Diff in Diff:** [How differencing twice isolates the treatment effect by removing fixed differences across units (Treated vs. Control) and fixed changes over time (Post vs. Pre).](https://josephessig-source.github.io/pols1600_site/slides/07-slides.html#/how-can-we-estimate-the-effect-of-moving-pumps-upstream) - **Average Treatment on Treated (ATT):** [The specific causal quantity estimated](https://josephessig-source.github.io/pols1600_site/slides/07-slides.html#/average-treatment-on-treated) ($E[Y_{1i}(1) - Y_{0i}(1)|D=1]$). - **Parallel Trends Assumption:** The crucial identifying assumption that, absent treatment, the treated group would have followed the exact [same trajectory as the control group.](https://josephessig-source.github.io/pols1600_site/slides/07-slides.html#/identifying-assumption-of-a-difference-in-differences-design) - **Regression Implementation:** [How to estimate DiD using a linear model](https://josephessig-source.github.io/pols1600_site/slides/07-slides.html#/using-linear-regression-to-estimate-a-difference-in-difference) ($Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 Post + \beta_2 Treated + \beta_3 Post \times Treated$), where the interaction term ($\beta_3$) provides the ATT. ## The Law of Large Numbers (LLN) {.smaller} > As sample size increases, the sample mean converges to the true population mean You should know: - **The core intuition:** Why an unbiased estimate improves and its variance decreases as the sample size grows. - **Mathematical formulation:** How the distance between the sample mean and the population mean $\mu$ approaches 0 as $n \to \infty$.' See [these slides](https://josephessig-source.github.io/pols1600_site/slides/09-slides.html#/the-law-of-large-numbers) ## The Central Limit Theorem (CLT) {.smaller} > The sampling distribution of the mean approaches a Normal distribution as sample size grows, regardless of the population's underlying distribution You should know: - **Sampling distributions:** What they are and how their width (variance) decreases as sample size increases. - **Standardization:** How to calculate and interpret Z-scores ($Z=\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}$). - **Properties of the sample mean:** Understanding that $E[\bar{X}_n]=\mu$ and $Var[\bar{X}_n]=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}$. - **Normal approximation:** How the CLT allows us to conduct statistical inference regardless of the shape of the population distribution. See [these slides](https://josephessig-source.github.io/pols1600_site/slides/09-slides.html#/the-central-limit-theorem) ## Standard Errors and Variance {.smaller} > Standard errors quantify uncertainty by estimating the standard deviation of a sampling distribution You should know: - **Variance of regression coefficients:** How it depends on the residuals in your model. - **Homoskedasticity vs. Heteroskedasticity:** Recognizing the difference between constant error variance ($\sigma^2$) and non-constant error variance. - **Robust Standard Errors:** Why we use functions like `lm_robust()` to calculate consistent standard errors (or cluster them by group) when error variance is not constant. See [these slides](https://josephessig-source.github.io/pols1600_site/slides/09-slides.html#/lab-8-and-standard-errors) ## Estimating Uncertainty: Simulation vs. Analytic > Bootstrapping can be used to obtain a standard error and confidence intervals using resampling. To make inferences about a population, we need to understand the sampling distribution and Standard Error (SE). There are two main ways to do this: - **Simulation (Bootstrapping):** Treat your observed sample as if it were the true population. Draw repeated samples *with replacement* to create a "resampling distribution." - **Calculating SE:** The Standard Error is the standard deviation of this simulated resampling distribution (the "plug-in principle"). - **Analytic (Asymptotic):** Relies on statistical theory (Law of Large Numbers & Central Limit Theorem), which state that sampling distributions approach a normal distribution as sample size grows. [See these slides](https://josephessig-source.github.io/pols1600_site/slides/10-slides.html#/calculating-standard-errors) ## Sampling Distributions and Statistical Inference - See also the earlier slides in this presentation on: - Confidence Intervals - Sampling Distributions - Hypothesis Testing - Statistical Power - Randomization Inference

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
